wingfield.text: The company largely preferred Archer's Hope for its ground and fresh water, but a ship could not lie against its bank.
wingfield.desc: An English gentleman in his late fifties, President of a colonial council: stiff, formal and proud, measured and a little pompous, a dry upper-class voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

kendall.text: It is that this must stay alight for the better part of a minute while you do six other things.
kendall.desc: An English soldier in his thirties, a captain: clipped, hard and gruff, short sentences, a low firm voice used to giving orders, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

gosnold.text: The work goes on, but it goes on slower, and it goes on with fewer eyes on the water.
gosnold.desc: An English sea captain of about thirty-five: warm, steady authority, confident and plain-spoken, a clear medium voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

smith.text: I have no love for the man who stole, but I have no love for the man who swung either.
smith.desc: A young English soldier of twenty-seven from Lincolnshire: brash, quick and sure of himself, energetic, a little impatient, a medium-high voice with a country edge, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

hunt.text: I would have them remember that a deer is a gift, and a gift is not a threat.
hunt.desc: An English clergyman in his late thirties: gentle, calm and warm, a soft and patient preacher's voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

laydon.text: And I am the one out in the trees with an axe while they could have shot me standing still.
laydon.desc: A young English labourer in his twenties from the country: plain, honest and tired, a rough rural accent, a medium voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

laxon.text: I have measured the timber for the storehouse and there is not enough to spare.
laxon.desc: An English carpenter in his thirties: practical, steady and dry-humoured, a Midlands working man's voice, medium-low, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

newport.text: This is a cape, not a colony, no depth for the ships and no cover from the sea.
newport.desc: An English sea captain in his late forties, master of a fleet: commanding and booming, a deep weathered voice that carries across a deck, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

percy.text: The six and twentieth day of April, about four in the morning, we descried the land of Virginia.
percy.desc: A young English aristocrat of twenty-six, a nobleman's son: refined, soft-spoken and precise, a light cultured voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

archer.text: Thirty of us ashore, and not a man among us knows what is in those trees.
archer.desc: An English gentleman of about thirty, trained in the law: articulate, sharp and quick, a crisp medium voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

clerk.text: It is written into their instructions - find a river that runs far into the land, and follow it up.
clerk.desc: An English company clerk in his forties: precise, dry and a little nasal, careful with every word, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

sailor.text: Then Spain came at England with the whole Armada, and every hull in the kingdom was pressed to the fight.
sailor.desc: An old English seaman in his fifties from the West Country: gravelly, weathered and rough, slow and knowing, a West Country burr, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

gent.text: He beams at you, delighted to be agreed with - and you notice he has no answer beyond the beaming.
gent.desc: A young English gentleman in his twenties seeking his fortune: eager, posh and a little arrogant, a bright upper-class voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

cook.text: That he was there first and had the better claim, and I could not fault his reasoning.
cook.desc: An English ship's cook in his forties: hoarse and grumbling, a rough working voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

boy.text: Mind yourself - cook's got a temper and a ladle, and he's quick with both.
boy.desc: An English ship's boy of about twelve: a young boy's high clear voice, quick and cheeky, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

snore.text: Somewhere under the snoring is the word gold.
snore.desc: A sleepy English sailor woken from sleep: mumbling, slow and drowsy, low and rough, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

sick.text: If I die out here, tell my brother he was right.
sick.desc: A seasick young English gentleman: weak, queasy and miserable, posh but faint, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

cooper.text: A good cask is worth three men on a crossing.
cooper.desc: An English cooper in his fifties who mends barrels: grumpy, gruff and impatient, a rough craftsman's voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

irons.text: When we land they'll open that sealed box and read out the Council.
irons.desc: An English prisoner held in chains below decks: hoarse, low, desperate and bitter, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

helmsman.text: In weather they come below and we work the tiller with tackles, four of us on the ropes.
helmsman.desc: A middle-aged English seaman at the helm: steady, terse and calm, a plain working voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

studley.text: Half a pint of wheat and half a pint of barley a man a day, boiled with water.
studley.desc: An English merchant clerk keeping a colony's store: careful, anxious and tired, counting every measure, a quiet precise middle voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

ratcliffe.text: He denied me a penny whittle, a chicken, a spoonful of beer, and served me with foul corn.
ratcliffe.desc: An English sea captain of the council, sick and resentful: bitter, aggrieved and blustering, a harsh middle-aged voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.

martin.text: My son is sick, and the President will not give him so much as a spoonful of beer above his allowance.
martin.desc: An English gentleman of the council, a father whose son is sick: grieving and angry, a strained older voice, an English accent of the early 1600s, not American.
